end.question: Hydrogen fluoride (HF) boils at 19.5 °C and hydrogen chloride (HCl) at −85 °C, although HCl is the heavier molecule. What is the main reason?

options.label: HF molecules form hydrogen bonds with one another
HF molecules are larger than HCl molecules
HF has a stronger covalent bond inside the molecule
HCl is not polar

end.explanation: Hydrogen on a highly electronegative atom like fluorine is drawn to a lone pair on the next molecule, a hydrogen bond, which beats the extra dispersion force of the heavier HCl.

end.question: Pulling a mole of liquid ethanol's molecules apart takes 38.6 kJ, and breaking the C–C bond in a mole of ethanol takes 348 kJ. What happens when ethanol boils?

options.label: The molecules separate and stay whole
The C–C bonds break and the pieces drift off
The O–H bonds break first
Both the molecules and their bonds separate

end.explanation: The heat only has to overcome the much weaker forces between molecules, so boiling leaves each molecule intact.

end.question: A diagram shows a sodium ion in water with the oxygen ends of the water molecules pointing at the ion. Which force does it show?

options.label: Ion–dipole
Dipole–dipole between two ions
London dispersion only
Covalent bonding

end.explanation: The negative ends of the polar water molecules point at the positive ion: an ion–dipole force.

end.question: Acetone's vapor pressure at 25 °C is about 31 kPa and water's is about 3 kPa. Which statement about their boiling points at sea level is most likely true?

options.label: Acetone boils at a higher temperature than water
Acetone boils at a lower temperature than water
They boil at the same temperature
Acetone cannot boil

end.explanation: The liquid with the higher vapor pressure at a given temperature reaches the outside pressure sooner as it is heated, so it boils at a lower temperature.

end.question: Ice floats on liquid water. Which statement explains why?

options.label: Ice molecules are lighter than liquid water molecules
Ice has weaker forces between its molecules than liquid water
Air bubbles trapped in ice always make it float
Hydrogen bonds hold ice's molecules in an open lattice, so ice is less dense than the liquid

end.explanation: The same molecules take up more space in the open hydrogen-bonded lattice of ice than they do in the liquid.

end.question: Liquid X has a higher surface tension than liquid Y at the same temperature. What does this suggest about the forces between their molecules?

options.label: The forces between X's molecules are weaker
The bonds inside X's molecules are stronger
The forces between X's molecules are stronger
X's molecules are lighter

end.explanation: Molecules at the surface are pulled inward by their neighbours. The stronger that pull, the higher the surface tension.

end.question: How much heat vaporizes 90.0 g of water at 100 °C? The heat of vaporization is 40.65 kJ/mol and the molar mass of water is 18.0 g/mol.

options.label: 203 kJ
732 kJ

end.explanation: 90.0 g is 5.00 mol, and 5.00 mol × 40.65 kJ/mol = 203 kJ, with no change of temperature.

end.question: What is the enthalpy change for 1 mol of steam condensing to water at 100 °C?

options.label: 0 kJ

end.explanation: Condensation is the reverse of vaporization, so it has the same size of enthalpy change with the opposite sign.

end.question: Beyond the exam: ice is warmed at a constant pressure of 0.3 kPa, which is below water's triple point pressure of 0.611 kPa. What happens?

options.label: It turns straight to vapour without becoming liquid
It melts at 0 °C, then boils
It stays solid at every temperature
It melts and boils at the same temperature

end.explanation: Below the triple point pressure there is no liquid region on water's phase diagram, so the solid becomes vapour directly.

end.question: 1.0 L of 0.10 M CaCl₂ and 1.0 L of 0.10 M sugar solution are compared. Which has more dissolved particles, and by how much?

options.label: CaCl₂, three times as many
CaCl₂, twice as many
The same number in each
Sugar, because its molecules are larger

end.explanation: Each CaCl₂ separates into Ca²⁺ and two Cl⁻, so 0.10 mol gives 0.30 mol of particles, while 0.10 mol of sugar stays as 0.10 mol of molecules.

end.question: Ammonium nitrate dissolves in water and the water gets colder. What does that show?

options.label: Dissolving is endothermic: energy flows into the dissolving process from the water
Dissolving is exothermic: energy flows out to the water
No energy changes when a solid dissolves
The solution has less mass than before

end.explanation: A falling temperature means energy left the water and went into the process, so dissolving this salt is endothermic.

end.question: What mass of NaCl (58.44 g/mol) is needed to make 500.0 mL of 0.200 M solution?
Which change makes new molecules?

options.label: Ice melting
Water boiling
Water being split into hydrogen and oxygen
A puddle freezing

end.explanation: Melting, boiling and freezing are phase changes: the molecules stay whole. Splitting water breaks its bonds and makes hydrogen and oxygen molecules.

end.question: Which statement describes a gas?

options.label: It takes the shape and volume of its container, and its molecules are far apart
It keeps its volume but takes the shape of its container
It keeps its own shape, with its molecules touching in fixed places
Its molecules touch one another but slide past each other

end.explanation: A gas has neither a definite shape nor a definite volume, because its molecules are far apart and move freely.

end.question: Why can a solution of salt in water not be separated by filtering?

options.label: The dissolved ions are too small to be held back by the paper
The salt is heavier than the water
Filter paper dissolves salt
Salt has no charge

end.explanation: The components of a liquid solution are mixed at the scale of single ions and molecules, so they pass through the pores of the paper together.

end.question: A mixture of acetone (boils at 56 °C) and water (boils at 100 °C) is slowly distilled. What does the first vial of liquid collected hold most of?

options.label: Acetone, because its molecules are held to one another less tightly
Water, because it is the lighter molecule
Equal parts of each, because they are mixed
Neither: nothing can be collected below 100 °C

end.explanation: The liquid with weaker forces between its molecules and the lower boiling point forms more of the vapour, so the first vial is richer in acetone.

end.question: Beyond the exam: 1.0 mol of each of sugar, NaCl and CaCl₂ is dissolved in its own 1.0 kg of water. Treating each as ideal, which boils at the highest temperature?

options.label: Sugar
NaCl
CaCl₂
They boil at the same temperature

end.explanation: The rise is i x K_b x m, and CaCl₂ makes three particles per formula unit against two for NaCl and one for sugar.

problems.question: A sealed jar of gas is squeezed into a third of its original volume. What happens to its molecules?

options.label: They stay the same size and the gaps between them shrink
Each molecule shrinks to a third of its size
Two thirds of the molecules disappear
The bonds inside the molecules break

problems.explanation: A gas is mostly empty space, so squeezing it only pushes the same molecules closer together. The molecules and their bonds are unchanged.

problems.question: A 1.00 L jar of liquid water weighs 1000 g and a 1.00 L jar of ice weighs 917 g. What does this say about the molecules?

options.label: Each molecule in the ice has a little more room
The molecules in ice are lighter
Ice molecules have fewer atoms
Ice molecules are broken into smaller pieces

problems.explanation: Both jars hold the same kind of molecule, so the lighter jar holds fewer of them in the same space. Each molecule in the ice has slightly more room.

problems.question: Which of these molecules can form hydrogen bonds with others of its own kind?

options.label: CH₄
CH₃OH
CO₂
PH₃

problems.explanation: In methanol a hydrogen is attached to oxygen, so it can be drawn to a lone pair on the next molecule. The other three have no H on N, O or F.

problems.question: Fluorine (F₂) is a gas at room temperature and iodine (I₂) is a solid. Both are nonpolar. What explains the difference?

options.label: Iodine's larger electron cloud is more polarizable, so its dispersion forces are stronger
Iodine molecules are polar
Iodine forms hydrogen bonds
Fluorine has a stronger bond than iodine

problems.explanation: Bigger electron clouds are easier to distort, so heavier nonpolar molecules attract their neighbours more strongly.

problems.question: Quartz and fused silica glass are both SiO₂. Quartz melts at 1713 °C, but the glass goes from rigid to runny over about 1040 to 1585 °C. What explains the difference?

options.label: Quartz's particles sit in a repeating pattern and the glass's do not
Quartz is an ionic solid and the glass is a metal
The glass is a molecular solid
The glass has no covalent bonds

problems.explanation: In a crystal every hold is alike, so all of them give way at one temperature. A glass is amorphous: its holds differ from place to place, so they give way a few at a time.

problems.question: Iodine (I₂) melts at 114 °C and sodium chloride at 801 °C. What does melting iodine have to overcome?

options.label: Only the weak forces between the I₂ molecules
The bond inside every I₂ molecule
The attraction between oppositely charged ions
The hold of a sea of free electrons

problems.explanation: Iodine is a molecular solid: whole molecules held by weak grips between them. Melting separates the molecules and leaves each I–I bond intact.

problems.question: Ethanol and water are each sealed in a flask at 25 °C. Ethanol's gauge settles at 7.9 kPa and water's at 3.2 kPa. What does this say about the forces between their molecules?

options.label: Ethanol's molecules are held to each other less strongly than water's
Ethanol's molecules are held to each other more strongly than water's
Ethanol has weaker bonds inside its molecules
The two liquids have the same forces and differ only in mass

problems.explanation: The weaker the forces between a liquid's molecules, the more of them escape into the vapor, so the higher its vapor pressure at the same temperature.

problems.question: Water boils at 100 °C at sea level. At the top of a high mountain the outside pressure is lower. What happens to the temperature at which water boils there?

options.label: It is higher, because thin air holds heat in
It stays at 100 °C, because that is a fixed property of water
It is lower, because the vapor pressure reaches the lower outside pressure sooner
Water cannot boil there

problems.explanation: A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the pressure outside it. A lower outside pressure is matched at a lower temperature.

worked.title: Gas Over Water at 40 °C
worked.setup: A gas is collected over water at 40 °C. The jar's gauge reads 98.0 kPa, and the vapor pressure of water at 40 °C is 7.4 kPa.

steps.say: What does the jar's gauge count?

options.label: The gas alone
The gas and the water vapor together
The water vapor alone

steps.hint: Everything in the jar pushes on the gauge.
steps.explain: The gauge reads the pressure of everything in the jar: the gas and the water vapor mixed with it.

steps.say: How much of the gauge is the water vapor?
steps.hint: Water's own pressure at the jar's temperature is given.
steps.explain: The water vapor pushes with its own vapor pressure at 40 °C, 7.4 kPa.

steps.say: What is the pressure of the gas alone?
steps.hint: The two pressures add up to the gauge.

steps.say: What percentage of the gauge is water vapor?
steps.hint: Divide the vapor's pressure by the gauge and multiply by 100.

steps.say: The water is warmed to 60 °C, where its vapor pressure is 19.9 kPa, and the gauge stays at 98.0 kPa. What happens to the gas alone?

options.label: It rises
It falls
It stays the same

steps.hint: The vapor takes a bigger share of the same gauge.
steps.explain: More of the gauge is water vapor, so the gas alone is 98.0 - 19.9 = 78.1 kPa.

worked.finish: The gauge is the gas plus the water vapor. Find the water's vapor pressure at the jar's temperature and take it from the gauge.

problems.question: On the heating curve of a pure substance, the line goes level for a while although heat is still being added. What is happening to the sample?

options.label: It is changing state, and the heat is spent loosening the attractions between its particles
The heat is being lost to the room
The thermometer has stopped working
The particles have stopped moving

problems.explanation: During a change of state the added heat works against the forces between particles, so their average motion, and the temperature, stays the same.

problems.question: 1.00 g of steam at 100 °C and 1.00 g of water at 100 °C each cool to 37 °C on a hand. Which gives the hand more heat, and why?

options.label: The steam, because it also gives out the heat of vaporization as it condenses
The water, because it is denser
They give the same, because both start at 100 °C
The water, because it cools more slowly

problems.explanation: Steam gives out about 2.26 kJ as it condenses, on top of the 0.26 kJ both give as the liquid cools from 100 °C to 37 °C.

worked.title: Ice to Warm Water
worked.setup: How much heat takes 36.0 g of ice at 0 °C to water at 25.0 °C? The heat of fusion of ice is 6.01 kJ/mol, the specific heat capacity of water is 4.184 J/(g·K) and the molar mass of water is 18.0 g/mol.

steps.say: How many moles of water are in 36.0 g?
steps.hint: Divide the mass by the molar mass.

steps.say: How much heat melts the ice at 0 °C?
steps.hint: Heat for a change of state is moles times the heat per mole.
steps.explain: 2.00 mol × 6.01 kJ/mol = 12.02 kJ. The temperature stays at 0 °C.

steps.say: How much heat then warms the 36.0 g of water from 0 °C to 25.0 °C?
steps.hint: q = m × c × ΔT, then change joules to kilojoules.

steps.say: What is the total heat added?
steps.hint: Add the melting and the warming.

steps.say: The same water is cooled back to ice at 0 °C. What is the heat change?

options.label: 0 kJ

steps.hint: Cooling and freezing are the way up run backwards.
steps.explain: Heat leaves the sample on the way down, so the heat change is -15.79 kJ.

worked.finish: Each level stretch of a heating curve costs moles times a heat per mole, each slope costs m × c × ΔT, and the way back gives out the same heat.

problems.question: A student adds water to 50.0 mL of a 0.800 M solution until it measures 200.0 mL. What is the new molarity?
problems.explanation: The moles of solute do not change when water is added: 0.800 M × 50.0 mL = M × 200.0 mL, so M = 0.200 M.

problems.question: Hexane dissolves wax but not table salt. Which explanation is best?

options.label: Salt is held by strong ion attractions that hexane's weak dispersion forces cannot replace, while wax and hexane both rely on dispersion forces
Hexane is too light to mix with salt
Salt melts at a higher temperature than hexane boils
Wax is a liquid at room temperature

problems.explanation: Substances with similar intermolecular interactions tend to dissolve in each other. Hexane cannot pull ions out of a salt crystal, but it mixes freely with a hydrocarbon such as wax.

worked.title: Make a Solution, Then Dilute It
worked.setup: 14.9 g of KCl (molar mass 74.55 g/mol) is dissolved in water and made up to 500 mL. Then 20.0 mL of that solution is made up to 100 mL with water.

steps.say: How many moles of KCl are in 14.9 g?
steps.hint: Divide the grams by the molar mass.

steps.say: What is the molarity of the 500 mL solution?
steps.hint: Molarity is moles per litre of solution, so change 500 mL to litres.

steps.say: How many moles of KCl are in the 20.0 mL taken out?
What is the molarity once that 20.0 mL is made up to 100 mL?
steps.hint: The moles are the same; the litres are now 0.100.

steps.say: How many moles of ions (K⁺ and Cl⁻ together) are in the 100 mL?
steps.hint: Each KCl gives two ions in water.
steps.explain: 0.00800 mol of KCl × 2 ions each = 0.0160 mol of ions.

worked.finish: Molarity counts the dissolved formula units in each litre. Adding water keeps the moles and lowers the molarity, and a salt that dissolves into ions puts more particles in the water than its moles of formula units.

problems.question: Ink is run on polar paper in a nonpolar solvent. Dye X stays near the start line and dye Y travels with the solvent front. What does this suggest?

options.label: X is more polar than Y, because the polar paper holds it more strongly than the nonpolar solvent does
Y is more polar than X, because it moves further
X and Y have the same polarity but different masses
The two dyes are the same substance

problems.explanation: A polar dye is held by polar paper and is poorly carried by a nonpolar solvent, so it stays low. A chromatogram is read this way to infer relative polarities.

problems.question: A salt solution is poured through filter paper and a drop of the filtrate is left to dry on glass. What is left on the glass?

options.label: Nothing, because filter paper removes the salt
A white crust of salt, because the dissolved salt passed through the paper
Sand grains from the paper
Pure water

problems.explanation: Dissolved ions are far smaller than the pores of the paper, so they pass through with the water and are left behind when the water dries off.

worked.title: Reading a Chromatogram
worked.setup: A paper strip runs until the solvent front is 12.5 cm above the start line. The centre of a dye's spot is 8.0 cm above the start line. A second dye in the same run has an Rf of 0.24.

steps.say: What is the Rf of the first dye?
steps.hint: Rf is the spot's distance divided by the front's distance, both from the start line.

steps.say: Which dye does the paper hold more strongly?

options.label: The dye with Rf 0.24
The dye with Rf 0.64
Neither: Rf says nothing about how strongly paper holds a dye

steps.hint: A dye that is held strongly is carried less far by the liquid.
steps.explain: The lower Rf means the dye stayed nearer the start line, so the paper held it more strongly than the liquid carried it.

steps.say: How far from the start line is the second dye's spot, in cm?
steps.hint: Distance = Rf times the front's distance.

steps.say: The strip is run again on a longer sheet until the front is 15.0 cm. How far from the start line is the first dye's spot, in cm?
steps.hint: The Rf of a dye in one solvent does not change with the length of the run.

worked.finish: Rf is a ratio of two distances, so it stays the same however far the front runs, and it can be used to predict a spot's height on a longer strip.
